snippets.snippet_text: The Hebrew word keritut ('divorce') derives from the root meaning 'to cut'—referring to the covenant being severed. God's rhetorical question in Isaiah 50:1 ('Where is the bill of divorcement?') invokes Deuteronomy's legal requirement, turning Israel's complaint of abandonment back on themselves: no formal document exists because God has not divorced them.

In Isaiah 50:4, the Servant declares he has been given 'the tongue of the learned'—literally 'the tongue of disciples.' This wasn't innate genius but systematic spiritual formation. The parallel to Isaiah 42:1-4's first Servant Song shows that true authority comes through disciplined instruction, not independent mastery.

Isaiah 50:5's 'opened ear' echoes Exodus 21:5-6, where a slave voluntarily enters permanent service by having his ear pierced. The Servant's willing submission to God mirrors this ancient legal ritual—making his obedience not coerced but chosen, which deepens the paradox of his coming suffering.

The Dead Sea Scrolls preserve a stunning variant reading in Isaiah 53:11: instead of 'he shall see the travail of his soul and be satisfied,' some manuscripts read 'he shall see light and be satisfied.' This single word difference shifts the emphasis from the Servant's anguish to his ultimate revelation and vindication.

Isaiah 54:5 stacks six divine titles and describes God as Zion's 'Maker' (creator) and 'Husband' (covenant partner). This extraordinary claim—that the God who fashioned creation is also the one bound in marital covenant to Israel—finds its complete expression in temple theology and sealing ordinances.

Isaiah 53:6 uses a shepherd-and-sheep metaphor to universalize vicarious atonement: 'all of us like sheep have gone astray...and the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all.' The pastoral image connects to the scapegoat ritual (Leviticus 16) where one animal bears Israel's collective sins, making Isaiah's Servant the ultimate fulfillment of Old Testament atonement theology.
